run.market_summary: 1) Democrats' sweeping midterm win (House and Senate) is the dominant story. It triggered a relief rally led by consumer discretionary and a sharp oil selloff, but futures are now flat, so the easy move looks done. Tariff-rollback talk is mostly rhetoric: any repeal still faces a presidential veto. 2) Rates and inflation are hawkish but the signal is noisy. Headlines conflict on whether the Fed hiked or held. Inflation is at a 3-year high, eurozone CPI is at 4%, and JOLTS and ADP are strong. The Senate result also blocks a dovish Fed overhaul. Against that, crude down ~13% in a week is disinflationary and long bonds have rallied. 3) Tail risks the rally ignores: Taiwan reports a massive PLA naval mobilisation, and the Iran war remains unresolved even as Vance blames it for the election loss.

ideas.thesis: Qualcomm fell 7% on a weak forecast blamed on a memory shortage hurting smartphone sales. That is a supply-chain problem that will not clear in one quarter, and guidance cuts tend to keep drifting lower as analysts revise numbers down. The stock has not been lifted by the election relief bid in megacaps.

Several things point to higher long-end yields: a Fed turning hawkish (rate hike reported, inflation at a 3-year high), hot labor data (JOLTS openings up sharply, ADP beat), and eurozone CPI at 4% pushing the ECB toward hikes. TLT rose 1% this week on the oil collapse, which gives a better entry. Size is small because the signal is ambiguous.

analysis.headline: A blue-wave backlash against the AI build-out erased Wednesday's post-midterm rally: semis lost 11.6%, the S&P 500 fell 4.4% (its worst day since April 2025) and the VIX jumped 70% to about 28. Bonds caught a modest bid and the dollar and gold barely moved.
analysis.narrative:
This was an equity-specific liquidation of the AI trade, not a macro panic. Before the open, the move was confined to AI hardware: SMH opened 4.5% lower, AMD 7.9%, LRCX 6.1% and QCOM 13.2% (on earnings). SPY opened only 0.17% lower, and DIA, XLF, XLC and XLP opened higher. The damage came during the session. SPY fell another 4.2% after the open, and all 13 sector ETFs closed red. The AP, Fox Business, Reuters, Motley Fool and Bloomberg all tie the selloff to Democrats' midterm sweep. Their reading: anti-data-center campaigns, ballot measures that went against data centers in nearly every case (CNBC 13:08), and calls to pause projects as power prices rise mean a slower, costlier AI build-out. MarketWatch had flagged this at 16:55 on 11/04 ("election results strike at the core of data-center optimism"). IREN's report of $4B in delayed annualized revenue (CNBC 18:25 / Reuters 18:49) was a reported customer delay, not a political one, and it supports the same story. Memory and storage names were hit hardest (SanDisk -22%, Micron -17%, WDC -17%), along with AMD -17.7%, LRCX -16.6% (despite a $25B buyback), AMAT -13.6%, AVGO -10.5% and NVDA -9.3%. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% and is now in correction.

The selloff spread through every link of the AI supply chain. Power and infrastructure names fell (GEV, PWR, CAT -6.4%, PAVE -5.8%, NUE -8.3%, FCX -7.5%), as did EEM -5.8%, which is heavy in Korea and Taiwan chipmakers. High-beta names went with them: ARKK -9%, TSLA -10.8% (which also carries Musk/political risk), crypto (IBIT -5%, COIN and MSTR about -9.5%) and HOOD -10%. The hyperscalers that pay for the build-out held up much better: GOOGL -2.2%, AMZN -2.1%, AAPL -1.5%, XLC -0.55% (z -0.4). That pattern fits a market cutting supplier revenue expectations, which would actually help buyers' free cash flow. Staples and utilities fell less than 1%, which is within normal noise.

Other assets were consistent with that reading. The 10-year fell 6bp to 4.84% (z -1.0, noise-level) and the 2-year fell about 12bp, as December Fed-hike odds slipped from the low 80s to about two-thirds. Thursday's data was also benign: unit labor costs -0.7% against +0.6% expected, productivity +3.6%, claims 189k. The dollar was flat and gold was flat, so this was not a global flight to safety. Oil's +3.5% all came before the open (Hormuz tanker attacks, uncertain Iran diplomacy) and it was flat during the session, yet XLE still fell 2.9%: energy stocks were sold with everything else. ITA's -68% is a forward stock split that took effect today. On a split-adjusted basis, defense lost about 3-4%, partly on reports that the $1.5T defense budget request now looks doomed.

analysis.cross_asset_read: This was a selloff inside equities, not a macro risk-off. VIX +70% (z +7.5) and all 13 sector ETFs fell. But the dollar was flat, gold was flat and the 10-year fell only 6bp (z -1.0), so no global flight to safety. The 2-year's 12bp drop is the main signal outside equities: markets priced fewer Fed hikes on growth and risk worries, and today's falling unit labor costs supported that. Oil's gain all came before the open (Hormuz) and isn't linked to the equity selloff. Energy stocks fell anyway. Within equities, suppliers (semis, memory, semicap, power and infrastructure, copper and steel) fell far more than the hyperscalers that buy from them. That points to a repricing of AI capex volumes, not a rates shock: yields fell while growth stocks crashed, which rules out rates as the driver.

model_grade.summary: Poor. The model treated the midterm result as a completed relief trade and missed that the same event threatened the AI build-out, the biggest equity theme. Its tilts on rates and oil were both wrong today. The QCOM short made money, but only from the opening gap.

lessons: When a political event lands, score its sector-specific policy effects separately from the broad relief read. A Democratic sweep should have raised tech_regulation for AI infrastructure (data-center pauses, power prices), not just been scored as a gridlock-is-good relief trade.

Weight 'contrarian' headlines that are published right after the close (e.g., MarketWatch 16:55, chip stocks slipping on election results) more heavily when the group already shows a weak 5-day trend; SMH was already falling.
Disambiguate central banks: 'interest rates expected to rise' from BBC Business is the BoE. Require the institution name before scoring Fed monetary_policy.
After a +3% index day driven by an event, add a reversal-risk flag when futures are flat overnight and one sector (semis) is opening lower before the open.
Screen anomaly lists for corporate actions (splits) before treating z-scores as real; ITA's z -49 was a 3:1-type split.
For short-TLT ideas, require confirmation from the 2-year and Fed pricing; in risk-off equity routs the front end rallies even with hawkish data in the background.
